name: Van Hilleary
primary_label: Republican Primary · U.S. House TN-6 (Open Seat)
bio: Former four-term U.S. Rep and 2002 GOP gubernatorial nominee. Was Rose's chief of staff, bringing D.C. experience to the open primary.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Congressional record (1995–2003) shows support for school choice via vouchers and accountability testing; no stated position on early childhood or pre-K in the current 2026 campaign.
early_childhood_ed.details: During his four terms in Congress, Hilleary voted YES on the No Child Left Behind Act of 2001 and YES on school choice vouchers (1997, 1998), reflecting a school-choice philosophy. His 2026 campaign emphasizes 'Veteran. Conservative. Fighter.' with Public Safety, Affordability, Freedom, and Energy priorities — with no specific platform on early childhood or pre-K education. He has raised $840,716 for the TN-6 race. No 2026 campaign statements on early childhood education or pre-K have been found. As of June 2026, his campaign website (vanfortn.com) contains only general Trump-support messaging with no issue-specific positions on childhood education.

child_hunger.summary: No public position found on child hunger in the 2026 campaign; 1994 Contract with America included welfare cuts that limited AFDC benefits.
child_hunger.details: No 2026 public statements linking Hilleary to child hunger, food insecurity, or SNAP were found. His 2026 campaign does not address these topics in available press coverage. His historical record from the 1990s includes support for the Contract with America, which included welfare reform measures. As of May 2026, he has raised $840,716 for the TN-6 race but has not issued public statements on federal nutrition programs.

parental_support.summary: Supported the child tax credit expansion and family tax relief in Congress; signed Contract with America's Families Reinforcement Act for child support enforcement and parental rights. No 2026 specific positions on modern PFML/childcare.
parental_support.details: In 2001, Hilleary voted YES on reducing the marriage tax penalty by $399 billion over 10 years (HR 6), which doubled the child tax credit for married couples. He signed the Contract with America's Families Reinforcement Act in 1994. His 2026 campaign platform has not published specific positions on paid family leave, modern childcare costs, or current child tax credit policy. His 2026 messaging focuses on Trump support, border security, and conservative values.

name: Johnny Garrett
primary_label: Republican Primary · U.S. House TN-6 (Open Seat)
bio: State legislator from Goodlettsville. First to file petitions; raised $1.1M with $1M+ cash on hand. Strong grassroots support.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Sponsored HB 1175 in the Tennessee legislature, related to childcare and school property leasing; supports the Education Freedom Scholarship expansion to 40,000 students (March 2026 Capitol Report); reported on school nutrition bill banning petroleum-based dyes. No federal pre-K or Head Start position. Controversy emerged in March 2026 over use of state funds for constituent mailers tied to congressional campaign.
early_childhood_ed.details: In his March 13, 2026 Tennessee House Capitol Report, Garrett reported on HB 2532, which would expand the Education Freedom Scholarship program to allow up to 40,000 students to use state education funds at nonpublic schools beginning in the 2026-27 school year. He also reported on HB 1853, which passed the House and bans petroleum-based artificial dyes from school meals — framing it as prioritizing children's health. As TN House Majority Whip, he sponsored HB 1175, which relates to childcare providers leasing school district property, signaling engagement with childcare access at the state level. His congressional campaign platform lists America First priorities with no mention of early childhood education or pre-K at the federal level. A March 2026 Tennessee Lookout report found he used state legislative funds for constituent mailers in his Sumner County district ahead of his federal run, raising ethics questions.

child_hunger.summary: No position on SNAP or child hunger in 2026 campaign. His April 2026 Capitol Report highlights HB 1853 banning petroleum-based dyes from school meals. Campaign platform focuses on border, economy, taxes, Second Amendment.
child_hunger.details: Garrett's April 10, 2026 Capitol Report highlights HB 1853, which passed the Tennessee House and bans petroleum-based artificial dyes from public school meals, framed as promoting children's health. This is the closest thing to a child nutrition position in his record but is a food safety/additive issue rather than a food access/hunger issue. No 2026 public statements or campaign positions on SNAP, Summer EBT, school lunch funding, or child food insecurity were found. His congressional campaign platform centers on lowering taxes, securing borders, supporting Trump's America First agenda, and conservative family values.

parental_support.summary: April 2026 Capitol Report highlights HB 2502 directing international money transfer tax revenue toward affordable childcare via the Promising Futures Fund. Voted NO on easing child-support payment requirements tied to felony voting rights restoration (April 2026). Sponsored HB 2449 requiring public libraries to adopt formal materials reconsideration policies. No specific federal PFML/CTC/childcare positions in congressional campaign.
parental_support.details: Garrett's April 10, 2026 Capitol Report highlights HB 2502, which directs revenue from an international money transfer tax toward expanding access to affordable childcare through the Promising Futures Fund and affordable housing — a state-level action. The same report notes HB 2350 ensuring foster parents are notified when parental rights petitions are filed. In April 2026, Garrett voted NO on a bill easing Tennessee's requirement that people with felony records fully pay child support arrears before voting rights restoration, expressing concern that child support arrearages could still be owed. He also sponsored HB 2449, requiring Tennessee public libraries to formally process residents' requests to reconsider collection items — framed in a parental rights and community standards context. His congressional campaign describes him as a Christian husband and father of three with conservative family values. No specific federal PFML, child tax credit, or childcare subsidy positions have been stated in his congressional campaign.

name: Dale Braden
primary_label: Republican Primary · U.S. House TN-6 (Open Seat)
bio: Republican primary candidate. Campaign suspended — confirmed by Tennessee Conservative News; campaign website is offline.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No public position found on early childhood education; campaign website lists no education policy. Campaign suspended.
early_childhood_ed.details: Braden's campaign website identified him as a 'conservative candidate' and 'political outsider' running on border security, lower inflation, protecting Social Security and Medicare, strengthening the military, and opposing the 'radical left's agenda.' Education policy, including early childhood education or pre-K, was not mentioned. His campaign has since been suspended, per Tennessee Conservative News, and the campaign website is offline.

child_hunger.summary: No public position found on child hunger or food assistance programs. Campaign suspended.
child_hunger.details: Braden's campaign platform did not address child nutrition, SNAP, WIC, or school meal programs. His stated priorities were immigration/border security, inflation, Social Security/Medicare, military, and opposing the progressive agenda. Campaign subsequently suspended.

parental_support.summary: No public position found on paid family leave, child tax credit, or childcare costs. Campaign suspended.
parental_support.details: Braden's campaign rhetoric referenced protecting against 'the radical left's agenda' and his opposition to transgender athletes in women's sports, sometimes framed in parental-rights terms. No explicit positions on paid family leave, child tax credits, childcare subsidies, or parental rights in education were identified before his campaign was suspended.

name: Mike Croley
primary_label: Democratic Primary · U.S. House TN-6 (Open Seat)
bio: Democratic candidate facing a steep climb in this strongly Republican district.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Supports public education investment and paying teachers fairly; wife works in local school system; no specific pre-K or childcare position found in 2026 campaign materials. Campaign now operating from mikefortn6.com in addition to croleyforcongress.com.
early_childhood_ed.details: Croley is a Navy veteran, former federal employee, and environmental engineer running as a Democrat in TN-6. His campaign emphasizes public education and paying teachers fairly, reflecting that his wife works in the local school system. He describes himself as passionate about public education and rural revitalization. No specific positions on pre-K, Head Start, or federal childcare subsidies were found in his 2026 campaign materials through June 2026. His AAA Blueprint focuses on affordability, accessibility, and accountability, but does not enumerate early childhood education specifically. He faces a crowded Democratic primary field in the August 6 primary.

child_hunger.summary: Explicitly opposes SNAP/WIC cuts and calls for overturning the One Big Beautiful Bill to restore nutrition funding; advocates taxing the wealthy to fund social programs. Has 'heard from parents who've had to dig into their savings because cuts to SNAP and WIC threaten to leave their families hungry.'
child_hunger.details: Croley's campaign states he has heard from parents who have had to dig into their savings because cuts to SNAP and WIC threaten to leave their families hungry. He calls for overturning the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — which cut SNAP by approximately $187 billion over 10 years — to restore funding to programs helping people meet basic needs. His broader AAA Blueprint ('Affordability, Accessibility, Accountability') focuses on lowering costs for families including groceries and healthcare. He frames himself as fighting for working families left behind by current policy. The 2026 Vanderbilt Child Health Poll found over a third of Tennessee families lack consistent access to food, and Tennessee did not participate in Summer EBT in 2026, reinforcing the salience of his position.

parental_support.summary: Supports fair wages, healthcare access, and protecting family support programs; opposes One Big Beautiful Bill cuts; no specific PFML/CTC positions found.
parental_support.details: Croley's campaign platform centers on fighting for working families, veterans, and teachers who are being left behind. He supports fair wages and broad healthcare access and opposes cuts to family support programs under the One Big Beautiful Bill. His AAA Blueprint addresses affordability and lowering costs for families. No specific positions on paid family and medical leave, child tax credit expansion, or childcare subsidies were found in his 2026 campaign materials beyond general opposition to benefit cuts and support for social investment.

name: Matt Van Epps
bio: Won the December 2025 special election after Mark Green's resignation. West Point graduate, combat veteran, and former state commissioner.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No position on early childhood education or childcare; supports school choice; opposes gender-affirming care for minors as parental rights framing. Sits on House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology and Homeland Security. No new early childhood education activity found through June 2026.
early_childhood_ed.details: Van Epps's campaign issues page and congressional office do not list positions on pre-K, Head Start, or federal childcare programs. He supports school choice and policies allowing education funding to follow students to private or charter schools. He frames his education stance around parental rights and opposes gender ideology in schools. No statements on early childhood education were found in his congressional press releases or newsletters through June 2026. His June 2026 press releases focus on the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve (American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026) and the NASA Reauthorization Act — neither related to education or childcare. FY2026 appropriations funded Head Start at $12.36 billion and the Child Care and Development Fund at $8.83 billion, but Van Epps has not commented publicly on either.

child_hunger.summary: Voted YES on Nutritious SNAP Act 2025 (March 4, 2026); voted YES on 2026 Farm Bill (S.4465, April 30, 2026) which preserves all OBBB SNAP cuts. Campaigned in support of the One Big Beautiful Bill during 2025 special election though was not in Congress when it passed. No new child hunger votes or statements found through June 2026.
child_hunger.details: Van Epps voted Yea on Roll Call Vote 155 (April 30, 2026) on S.4465, the 2026 Farm Bill (Farm, Food, and National Security Act), which passed 261-111 and reauthorizes SNAP through 2031 while cementing the SNAP cuts enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill. He described himself as a supporter of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act during his 2025 special election campaign; that law cut SNAP by approximately $187 billion over 10 years, expanded work requirements to adults up to age 64 and parents of children 14 and older, and required states to share program costs. He was not in Congress when the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in May 2025 but campaigned in support of it. No additional public statements specifically addressing child hunger in Tennessee were found through June 2026. Save the Children urged Congress to strengthen child protections in the Farm Bill as it advanced in March 2026, but Van Epps has not publicly responded to those calls.

parental_support.summary: Introduced bipartisan HONOR Gold Star Families Act (H.R. 7932, March 2026) doubling the military death gratuity from $100,000 to $200,000 for families of fallen servicemembers. Republican Study Committee (Feb 2026). Opposes government-funded gender surgeries for minors. No new family support legislation identified through June 2026.
parental_support.details: Van Epps introduced the bipartisan HONOR Gold Star Families Act (H.R. 7932, March 12, 2026) alongside Reps. Jen Kiggans and Jill Tokuda, doubling the military death gratuity from $100,000 to $200,000 for families of fallen servicemembers and adding a cost-of-living adjustment, applied retroactively to January 2026. This remains the most concrete family-support legislation he has introduced. He is married with a young daughter. His issues page opposes government-funded gender surgeries for minors and frames children's welfare in terms of protection from gender ideology. No positions on paid family and medical leave, child tax credit, or civilian childcare subsidies have been stated in 2026 campaign or congressional materials through June 2026. His June 2026 legislative activity focused on the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and NASA Reauthorization — unrelated to parental support policy.

name: Aftyn Behn
bio: Progressive activist who ran in the 2025 TN-7 special election, losing by 8.8 points while overperforming the 2024 baseline by 12.6 points. Withdrew from the 2026 TN-7 congressional race on January 12, 2026, citing safety concerns; is instead seeking re-election to her TN House District 51 seat.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Explicitly supported expanding early childhood care and investing in public education as core priorities during her TN-7 congressional campaign.
early_childhood_ed.details: During her TN-07 congressional run, her platform included 'Expand early childhood care and workforce pathways' as a named priority under 'Education & Caregiver Support.' As a Tennessee State Representative on the TN House Education Instruction Committee, she has consistently advocated for public investment in education over privatization. She withdrew from the 2026 congressional race on January 12, 2026.

child_hunger.summary: Campaign slogan 'feed kids, fix roads, fund hospitals' signaled child hunger as a top priority; supports eliminating Tennessee's regressive grocery tax.
child_hunger.details: Behn has led efforts in the Tennessee legislature to eliminate the state grocery tax, a direct measure to reduce food insecurity for low-income families with children. Her platform emphasized cutting costs of living, and her social work background directly engaged her with food-insecure populations. Her stated mission to 'feed kids' was one of three top-line commitments. She withdrew from the congressional race on January 12, 2026, citing safety concerns.

parental_support.summary: Supported expanding childcare access, protecting caregivers and educators, and defending reproductive rights as interconnected parental support issues during her congressional campaign.
parental_support.details: Her congressional platform called for expanding early childhood care and workforce pathways, paying and protecting caregivers, and investing in public education. She supports reproductive freedom and access to affordable healthcare. While paid family leave and the Child Tax Credit were not explicitly named, her progressive economic agenda aligns with support for these policies. She withdrew from the 2026 TN-7 congressional race on January 12, 2026, citing safety concerns; she is seeking re-election to her TN House District 51 seat instead.

name: David Kustoff
bio: Five-term incumbent attorney. Unopposed in Republican primary; $2.8M cash on hand.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Introduced bipartisan Child Care for American Families Act (H.R. 3155, 119th Congress) to expand the employer-provided childcare tax credit; no dedicated pre-K spending position. Voted NO on ARP (2021, included $39B childcare stabilization).
early_childhood_ed.details: Kustoff co-introduced H.R. 3155, the Child Care for American Families Act, in the 119th Congress alongside Reps. Claudia Tenney (R-NY), Brad Schneider (D-IL), and Terri Sewell (D-AL). The bill amends the IRC to enhance the Section 45F employer-provided childcare tax credit by increasing the credit amount, expanding access for small and rural businesses, and allowing employer consortia to jointly apply. Kustoff stated: 'In Tennessee, our economy is losing $2.6 billion annually because of insufficient access to childcare. This is a nationwide problem.' He voted NO on the American Rescue Plan (2021), which included $39 billion in childcare stabilization funding and expanded Head Start. He has no dedicated pre-K or public early education funding position on his issues page.

child_hunger.summary: Voted for One Big Beautiful Bill which cuts $267 billion from SNAP, voted against SNAP expansions in the American Rescue Plan, and publicly defended the SNAP cuts in a September 2025 op-ed calling characterizations of the cuts 'misinformation and frankly lies.'
child_hunger.details: Kustoff voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 4, 2025), which the CBO estimates will cut SNAP by approximately $267–287 billion over 10 years. New SNAP work requirements now apply to adults 55-64 and parents of school-age children 14 and older, groups previously exempt. In a September 22, 2025 op-ed on the Ways and Means Committee website, Kustoff defended the bill, calling characterizations of the SNAP cuts 'misinformation and frankly lies' and framing them as promoting self-sufficiency and fiscal responsibility. He voted NO on ARP SNAP expansions in 2021. He supported the 2018 Farm Bill reauthorization of child nutrition programs.

parental_support.summary: Supported enhanced and permanent Child Tax Credit ($2,200 per child) via OBBB; introduced bipartisan Child Care for American Families Act (H.R. 3155); voted NO on 2021 ARP CTC expansion; A+ pro-life rating January 2026.
parental_support.details: Through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Kustoff supported and helped advance via the Ways and Means Committee, the Child Tax Credit was permanently increased to $2,200 per child (up from $2,000) and indexed to inflation starting in 2026. Kustoff stated the bill 'boost[s] the doubled child tax credit.' He co-introduced the bipartisan Child Care for American Families Act (H.R. 3155) to expand employer childcare tax credits. He also co-introduced the bipartisan Save Struggling Hospitals Act with Rep. Terri Sewell (D-AL) in early 2026 to fix Medicare payment formulas for rural and lower-wage area hospitals — a measure affecting family healthcare access. He voted NO on the 2021 ARP CTC expansion and holds an A+ pro-life rating as of January 2026.

early_childhood_ed.details: Dewey Bryan is listed as a Democratic primary candidate in TN-8 on Ballotpedia and Tennessee Secretary of State filings, but no campaign website, social media presence, or policy platform was discoverable as of June 2026.

child_hunger.details: No campaign website, press releases, or news coverage detailing Bryan's position on SNAP, school meals, WIC, or childhood food insecurity was found.

parental_support.details: No statements on paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, childcare subsidies, or parental rights were found for Dewey Bryan. His candidacy is confirmed through official Tennessee election filings, but no public platform or media coverage of his policy positions was located.

name: Leonard Perkins
bio: Democratic primary candidate. Pastor and substance abuse counselor with 23 years of community service.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No explicit position found, though Perkins broadly commits to improving education access across all 19 counties of TN-8.
early_childhood_ed.details: Perkins's campaign website does not include early childhood education as a named priority. His stated issues include voting rights, women's rights, organized labor, veterans/survivors benefits, student debt, small businesses, and democracy. He criticizes incumbent Kustoff for inadequate support for education in the district's northern counties, indicating general support for increased federal education investment.

child_hunger.details: Perkins's campaign website does not list child hunger, SNAP, school meals, or food insecurity as a named priority. His platform focuses on veterans' rights, women's rights, and organized labor.

parental_support.summary: Supports women's reproductive autonomy and organized labor, which implicitly connect to parental support, but has not publicly stated positions on paid family leave, child tax credit, or childcare costs.
parental_support.details: His campaign explicitly lists 'Women's Rights' and 'Organized Labor' as top priorities. As a pastor and substance abuse counselor with 23 years of community service, his work has directly served families in crisis. However, no specific statement on the Child Tax Credit, paid family leave legislation, or childcare subsidy programs was located.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No specific public position on early childhood education found for her TN-8 congressional campaign. Her redistricting lawsuit was dismissed by a Tennessee state three-judge panel on May 26, 2026; federal challenges remain pending.
early_childhood_ed.details: Moses's published seven-point platform focuses on criminal justice reform, universal healthcare, food security, community health, environmental sustainability, youth violence prevention, and reparations. Youth-related planks include mentorship and leadership programs and investment in mental health services, but no explicit stance on pre-K, Head Start, childcare subsidies, or early learning programs. In May 2026, Moses filed a federal lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Tennessee challenging Tennessee's mid-election redistricting as unconstitutional, alleging the new maps were drawn after candidate filing deadlines had passed and that they split Memphis minority communities across multiple districts. On May 26, 2026, a three-judge state panel upheld Tennessee's redistricting and dismissed related lawsuits, with federal challenges still pending as of June 2026.

child_hunger.summary: Supports eliminating food deserts and promoting sustainable, local agriculture to improve food access in underserved communities. State redistricting lawsuit dismissed May 26, 2026; federal challenges remain.
child_hunger.details: Her platform calls for expanding farmers' markets in underserved areas to create direct farm-to-consumer channels, and for community education programs teaching people to grow their own food. She frames food security as central to community health. No explicit position on SNAP, WIC, school meal programs, or Summer EBT was found. Her May 2026 redistricting lawsuit noted the new congressional maps crack and split Memphis minority communities — the same communities most impacted by food insecurity — across multiple districts. The state court dismissed related redistricting lawsuits on May 26, 2026; federal challenges remain pending as of June 2026.

parental_support.summary: No specific public position on paid family leave, child tax credit, childcare costs, or parental rights found. State redistricting lawsuit dismissed May 26, 2026; federal challenges ongoing as of June 2026.
parental_support.details: Moses's platform emphasizes universal healthcare access, mental health investment, and economic opportunity for justice-impacted individuals, which would broadly benefit families. However, her published materials contain no explicit stances on federal paid family leave legislation, the Child Tax Credit, childcare cost reduction, or parental rights frameworks. Her most prominent public action in May-June 2026 involves the redistricting challenge. A Tennessee three-judge state panel dismissed related redistricting lawsuits on May 26, 2026, ruling the state is protected by sovereign immunity and that challengers did not establish distinct injury. Moses stated: 'What they did is unconstitutional — and I am not going to sit down I am going to stand up. This is not just about me. This is about every voter whose community is now being cracked and split across three separate congressional districts.' Federal legal challenges remain pending.

name: Horace Taylor
bio: Independent candidate. Describes himself as 'progressive in thought, yet grounded in principles and values.' $0 in FEC-reported contributions.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Identifies education as a personal passion in his Ballotpedia 2026 candidate survey; no specific early childhood education position found. Confirmed as independent candidate from Germantown on the TN-8 general election ballot.
early_childhood_ed.details: Taylor's Ballotpedia 2026 Candidate Connection survey identifies education as one of his key passions alongside cost of living and agriculture. He describes himself as 'progressive in thought, yet grounded in principles and values.' No campaign website or specific policy platform detailing his position on pre-K, Head Start, childcare subsidies, or early learning programs was publicly available as of June 2026. He is one of six independent candidates on the TN-8 general election ballot; the district carries a Cook PVI of R+21. FEC filings confirm $0 in contributions.

child_hunger.summary: No specific position found on child hunger; Ballotpedia survey identifies cost of living and agriculture as campaign focuses. No new statements found as of June 2026.
child_hunger.details: Taylor's Ballotpedia 2026 survey lists cost of living and agriculture among his top issues — areas adjacent to food access — but no specific statements on SNAP, WIC, school meals, or child nutrition programs were found in any June 2026 search. His independent candidacy has $0 in FEC contributions, limiting his public profile. Tennessee's 2026 legislative session ended without a permanent Summer EBT mandate, though $7 million was allocated for S-EBT beginning in 2027; Taylor made no public comment on this outcome.

parental_support.summary: No specific positions on paid family leave, child tax credit, childcare costs, or parental rights found.
parental_support.details: Taylor describes himself as 'progressive in thought, yet grounded in principles and values,' suggesting a moderate-to-progressive outlook, but no specific platform details on family support policy — paid leave, child tax credit, childcare — were publicly available as of May 2026.

name: Steve Cohen
bio: Ten-term incumbent and former state senator. $1.8M cash on hand; deep institutional support. ⚠ Tennessee signed a new congressional map May 7, 2026 that dismantles the old TN-9 (Memphis) and redraws it as a rural south Tennessee district. Cohen has filed a federal lawsuit challenging the map; the NAACP also filed separately. All candidates must refile by May 15. If the map survives legal challenge, Cohen faces a very difficult path in the redrawn district.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Longtime champion of Head Start, Early Head Start, and pre-K programs, securing tens of millions of dollars in federal grants for Memphis-area providers. Officially ended his campaign May 15, 2026 after redistricting; endorsed London Lamar in the TN-9 Democratic primary over Justin Pearson. Three-judge federal panel upheld new maps May 26, 2026; state court dismissed NAACP challenge. Cohen's political future now contingent on federal court reversal.
early_childhood_ed.details: Cohen has repeatedly championed Head Start grants for Memphis-area providers: $7.4 million to Shelby County Board of Education (April 2025), $35.5 million for Porter-Leath (July 2025), $2.6 million (December 2024), and $1.1 million for Early Head Start at Children's Bureau (2018). He co-sponsored H.R. 4318, the Head Start for Our Future Act, in the 119th Congress to strengthen and expand the program. He strongly opposed GOP efforts in 2015 to eliminate the Preschool Development Grant program, which he said would have cut $7 million from Shelby County Schools and denied preschool to nearly 7,500 low- and moderate-income Tennessee children. On May 15, 2026, he announced he would not seek re-election in any of the three gerrymandered districts carved from TN-9, stating Tennessee Republicans had 'silenced the Black vote in Memphis.' A Davidson County three-judge state court panel dismissed the NAACP-led state constitutional challenge, finding sovereign immunity barred claims against the Governor and General Assembly. A federal three-judge panel upheld the redistricting plan on May 26, 2026. Cohen endorsed state Sen. London Lamar over Justin Pearson in the TN-9 Democratic primary.

child_hunger.summary: Most vocal opponent of SNAP cuts in Tennessee congressional delegation. Condemned One Big Beautiful Bill Act SNAP cuts as 'likely the worst bill ever presented.' Co-sponsored Hunger-Free Future Act. Urged Gov. Lee to extend SNAP and restore Summer EBT. Only TN delegation member to vote NO on OBBB. Ended campaign May 15, 2026; endorsed London Lamar in TN-9 primary.
child_hunger.details: Cohen issued a statement after Senate passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill calling it 'a massive giveaway to the ultra-wealthy that slashes Medicaid and health care, makes the largest cuts to food assistance in American history.' He stated the SNAP cuts would gut food assistance 'for millions of children, seniors, and people with disabilities.' Cohen was the only member of the Tennessee delegation to vote against the legislation. He co-sponsored H.R. 2489, the Hunger-Free Future Act of 2025, which prohibits USDA updates to the Thrifty Food Plan that would increase food insecurity. He wrote to Gov. Lee urging emergency deployment of the state's $2 billion rainy-day fund to prevent SNAP disruptions for 690,000+ Tennesseans and called Tennessee's decision to opt out of Summer EBT 'cruel,' noting it denied $84 million in federal food aid to 700,000 children. Tennessee's 2026 session ended without a permanent Summer EBT mandate; $7 million was allocated for S-EBT starting in 2027. Cohen announced on May 15, 2026 that he will not seek re-election after redistricting. He endorsed state Sen. London Lamar in the TN-9 Democratic primary over Justin Pearson.

parental_support.summary: Persistent cosponsor of FAMILY Act for national paid family leave; voted February 2024 to expand Child Tax Credit for 79,000 Memphis children; voted NO on OBBB. Retired from race May 15, 2026; endorsed London Lamar over Pearson. Federal three-judge panel upheld redistricting May 26, 2026; consolidated federal litigation ongoing.
parental_support.details: Cohen has continuously cosponsored the Family and Medical Insurance Leave (FAMILY) Act, which would create a permanent, national paid family and medical leave program. In February 2024 he voted for H.R. 7024, a bipartisan bill expanding the Child Tax Credit's refundability, which he estimated would benefit 79,000 children in Memphis and TN-9. He voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. On May 15, 2026, Cohen announced he would not seek re-election after the Republican-led redistricting dismantled TN-9. A federal three-judge panel upheld Tennessee's new congressional maps on May 26, 2026. Three separate federal lawsuits — by the ACLU, the NAACP, and the League of Women Voters — were consolidated before Chief U.S. District Judge William Campbell Jr. and remain pending as of June 2026. Cohen endorsed state Sen. London Lamar in the TN-9 Democratic primary.

name: Justin J. Pearson
bio: Progressive challenger known for the Byhalia Pipeline fight and the 2023 'Tennessee Three' gun-protest expulsion. Pledging no corporate PAC money; raised $374K in Q1 2026 alone, narrowly outraising Cohen that quarter. Justice Democrats endorsed; pledged $1M through Leaders We Deserve. ⚠ The new map signed May 7 dismantles the Memphis-based TN-9; Pearson's brother KeShaun was arrested protesting at the Capitol. All candidates must refile by May 15; Pearson's campaign path in the redrawn district is unclear pending legal challenges.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Strongly backs public school funding, ending private school vouchers, and increased investment in Title I schools; mother taught public school 23 years. Actively campaigning in redrawn TN-9 as of June 2026. Faces primary challenge from state Sen. London Lamar, who was endorsed by outgoing Rep. Steve Cohen. Three-judge federal panel upheld redistricting May 26; federal litigation consolidated and ongoing.
early_childhood_ed.details: On his campaign issues page Pearson calls for demanding 'more funding to Title I schools like my alma mater, Mitchell High School, for technology, textbooks, and trades' and pledges to 'pass a national law that ends private school vouchers which serve as welfare checks for the wealthy.' He frames educational equity as a central pillar, noting his mother has been a public school teacher for 23 years. In a May 27, 2026 Time magazine profile, Pearson confirmed he is still running in the redrawn 9th district, stating that 'the issues facing voters did not disappear when Republicans remade the political terrain.' Tennessee stripped him of all committee assignments as punishment for redistricting protests. A three-judge federal panel upheld the new maps on May 26, 2026; three consolidated federal lawsuits remain pending. No specific early childhood education bill identified in his TN House record.

child_hunger.summary: Introduced HB1339 (2023) requiring Tennessee to seek federal funds to alleviate childhood hunger; congressional campaign calls for doubling the EITC and ending grocery tax; ActBlue page explicitly calls for pushing Congress to expand SNAP benefits. Actively campaigning in redrawn TN-9 as of June 2026. Endorsed by Justice Democrats with $1M pledge; opposed in primary by London Lamar (Cohen-endorsed).
child_hunger.details: As a state representative, Pearson introduced HB1339 in the 113th General Assembly, which would require the Tennessee Department to 'actively seek and apply for federal grants and other available federal funds, and utilize available federal funds, for the purpose of alleviating childhood hunger.' His campaign ActBlue page explicitly frames the campaign as 'pushing Congress to expand SNAP benefits' for struggling families. His congressional campaign platform cites that 33% of District 9 children live below the poverty line and pledges to double the Earned Income Tax Credit ('which would lift half of children in the country out of poverty') and end the grocery tax on working-class families. Tennessee's 2026 legislative session ended without a permanent Summer EBT mandate; $7 million was allocated for S-EBT starting in 2027.
